learning_goals: Explain what a large language model (LLM) is and its limits
Describe Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and its three steps
Show how RAG uses documents to give fresh, sourced answers

analogy.story: A student sits for an open‑book exam. The student first looks up the right page in the textbook, then writes the answer using that page.
analogy.mapping: Looking up the page = retrieval. Writing the answer from the page = generation.

worked_example.setting: A college student in Delhi uses a chatbot to check scholarship deadlines.
worked_example.question: What is the last date to apply for the National Scholarship 2024?
documents: National Scholarship 2024 applications close on 31 October 2024.
worked_example.retrieved: National Scholarship 2024 applications close on 31 October 2024.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: The last date to apply is 31 October 2024, according to the official scholarship notice.

sections.heading: ## What You Will Learn
points: You will explain what an LLM is and its limits (F1, F2, F3, F4).
You will define RAG and each word in its name (F5, F6).
You will list the three question‑time steps in order (F8).
You will name one benefit and one limitation of RAG (F11, F12).

sections.heading: ## Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Introduce AI, LLM, and why a plain LLM can be wrong.
points: A large language model (LLM) is an AI model trained on a very large amount of text (F1).
Training data is the collection of text the model learned from (F1).
Knowledge cutoff is the date after which the model knows nothing (F2).
Hallucination is when the model makes up facts that sound real (F4).
A prompt is the text you give the model to get an answer (F8).
A token is a word or part of a word the model reads (F1).

sections.heading: ## What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and the meaning of each word.
points: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (F5, F6).
Retrieval means finding relevant pieces of information (F5).
Augmented means adding those pieces to the prompt (F5).
Generation means the LLM writes the final answer (F5).

sections.heading: ## Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: Explain the main benefits of using RAG.
points: Answers can use up‑to‑date and private information (F11).
Fewer made‑up answers, though not zero (F11).
Answers can show their sources (F11).
No need to retrain the model; just update documents (F9, F11).
Cheaper and faster than fine‑tuning (F10, F11).

sections.heading: ## How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Describe preparation and the three question‑time steps.
points: Preparation: collect documents, split into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding using an embedding model, store in a vector database (F7).
An embedding model turns text into a list of numbers that capture meaning (F7).
An embedding is that list of numbers (F7).
A vector is the same list of numbers used for search (F7).
A chunk is a small piece of a document (F7).
A vector database holds embeddings for fast search (F7).
Semantic search finds chunks whose meaning matches the question (F8).
Question‑time step 1 Retrieve: turn the question into an embedding, fetch top‑k chunks (F8).
Step 2 Augment: place retrieved chunks into the prompt with an instruction (F8).
Step 3 Generate: the LLM writes the answer from the prompt (F8).
Only a limited amount of text fits in the prompt, called the context window (F12).

sections.heading: ## Example: College Scholarship Chatbot
sections.goal: Walk through a concrete Indian scenario.
points: Setting: student in Delhi asks a chatbot (worked_example.setting).
Question: last date for National Scholarship 2024 (worked_example.question).
Documents stored in the knowledge base (worked_example.documents).
Retrieval finds the snippet with the correct date (worked_example.retrieved).
Without RAG the LLM hallucinates a wrong date (worked_example.answer_without_rag).
With RAG the answer cites the correct date (worked_example.answer_with_rag).

sections.heading: ## Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: List the important terms with one‑line meanings.
points: large language model (LLM) – AI that predicts next token from huge text.
training data – text used to teach the model.
knowledge cutoff – date after which model knows nothing.
hallucination – model makes up false facts.
prompt – input text you give the model.
token – word or part of a word.
retrieval – finding relevant chunks.
augmented – adding chunks to the prompt.
generation – model writes the answer.
RAG – Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
embedding model – turns text into meaning numbers.
embedding – the meaning numbers.
vector – same as embedding.
chunk – small document piece.
vector database – stores embeddings for search.
semantic search – search by meaning.
context window – max text the prompt can hold.
fine‑tuning – extra training that changes model weights.
weights – internal numbers the model learns.
retraining – teaching the model again from scratch.

sections.heading: ## Quick Check
points: What does RAG stand for? – Retrieval-Augmented Generation.
Which step comes first at question time: retrieve, augment, or generate? – Retrieve.
Does RAG change the model’s weights? – No, it only adds documents.
Name one limitation of RAG. – Answer quality depends on retrieved chunks.

sections.heading: ## Summary
sections.goal: Recap the main ideas in plain language.
points: An LLM knows only its training data and can hallucinate.
RAG adds a retrieval step so the model uses fresh or private documents.
The three steps are retrieve, augment, generate, in that order.
Documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database.
RAG gives sourced, up‑to‑date answers without retraining the model.
The answer is only as good as the chunks retrieved.

quiz.q: What is the first step when a user asks a question in a RAG system?
quiz.a: Retrieve relevant chunks from the knowledge base

quiz.q: Does RAG modify the LLM's internal weights?
quiz.a: No, RAG does not change the model weights
The answer depends on the quality of the retrieved chunks
